theme: Suffering; elders; the roaring lion; grace is sufficient
readingInstruction: Read 1 Peter 4:1-5:14. Peter concludes by speaking of how to live in the face of suffering, how to use your gifts, how elders should lead, and how to resist the devil. Notice the repeated mention of grace and glory.
settingTheScene: Persecution against Christians was growing. Peter reminds his readers not to be surprised, since suffering is the normal path for those who follow the crucified Lord. He then gives instruction for the community: serve one another, elders shepherd the flock, the young submit, and all clothe themselves with humility. Peter, who was called to feed Christ’s sheep (John 21:15-17), writes now as a fellow elder.
observation: “Above all, keep loving one another earnestly, since love covers a multitude of sins” (4:8).
“As each has received a gift, use it to serve one another, as good stewards of God’s varied grace” (4:10).
“Beloved, do not be surprised at the fiery trial when it comes upon you to test you, as though something strange were happening to you” (4:12).
“But rejoice insofar as you share Christ’s sufferings, that you may also rejoice and be glad when his glory is revealed” (4:13).
“Shepherd the flock of God that is among you, exercising oversight, not under compulsion, but willingly, as God would have you” (5:2).
“Casting all your anxieties on him, because he cares for you” (5:7).
“Be sober-minded; be watchful. Your adversary the devil prowls around like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour” (5:8).
“And after you have suffered a little while, the God of all grace, who has called you to his eternal glory in Christ, will himself restore, confirm, strengthen, and establish you” (5:10).
interpretation:
Peter begins with a call to arm ourselves with the same way of thinking as Christ. “Since therefore Christ suffered in the flesh, arm yourselves with the same way of thinking, for whoever has suffered in the flesh has ceased from sin.” Suffering weans us from the old life. The time is past for doing what the Gentiles want, in sensuality and drunkenness; their surprise that you do not join them leads them to malign you. But they will give account to him who is ready to judge the living and the dead. “The end of all things is at hand; therefore be self-controlled and sober-minded for the sake of your prayers.”

Then the life of the church. “Above all, keep loving one another earnestly, since love covers a multitude of sins.” Show hospitality without grumbling. Every believer has a gift: “As each has received a gift, use it to serve one another, as good stewards of God’s varied grace: whoever speaks, as one who speaks oracles of God; whoever serves, as one who serves by the strength that God supplies, in order that in everything God may be glorified through Jesus Christ.” The gifts are for serving, and the aim is God’s glory.

Next, how to think about suffering: “Beloved, do not be surprised at the fiery trial when it comes upon you to test you, as though something strange were happening to you. But rejoice insofar as you share Christ’s sufferings, that you may also rejoice and be glad when his glory is revealed.” Suffering is not a sign that God has abandoned you; it is a share in Christ’s. “Blessed are you” if you are insulted for the name of Christ, for the Spirit of glory rests upon you. Only make sure you suffer for being a Christian and not for being a wrongdoer. “Yet if anyone suffers as a Christian, let him not be ashamed, but let him glorify God in that name.” The statement that judgment begins at the household of God (4:17) reminds us that God refines his own people first. Those who suffer according to God’s will should entrust their souls to a faithful Creator while doing good.

In chapter 5, Peter, “a fellow elder and a witness of the sufferings of Christ,” speaks to elders: “Shepherd the flock of God that is among you, exercising oversight, not under compulsion, but willingly, as God would have you; not for shameful gain, but eagerly; not domineering over those in your charge, but being examples to the flock. And when the chief Shepherd appears, you will receive the unfading crown of glory.” The younger are to be subject to the elders. All are to clothe themselves with humility, “for God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble.” “Humble yourselves, therefore, under the mighty hand of God so that at the proper time he may exalt you, casting all your anxieties on him, because he cares for you.”

The final warning: “Be sober-minded; be watchful. Your adversary the devil prowls around like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour. Resist him, firm in your faith, knowing that the same kinds of suffering are being experienced by your brotherhood throughout the world.” The devil is real and fierce, but he is a lion on a leash. Then comes the promise: “And after you have suffered a little while, the God of all grace, who has called you to his eternal glory in Christ, will himself restore, confirm, strengthen, and establish you. To him be the dominion forever and ever. Amen.” Peter signs off with greetings from Silvanus, from “she who is at Babylon” (the church in Rome), and from Mark, his son in the faith, with a final blessing: “Peace to all of you who are in Christ.”
connection: Romans 12:6-8 and 1 Corinthians 12 discuss spiritual gifts. Proverbs 10:12 is behind 4:8. Matthew 5:10-12 blesses those persecuted. Acts 5:41 shows the apostles rejoicing in suffering. Philippians 3:10 speaks of sharing Christ’s sufferings. Ezekiel 9:6 and Malachi 3:1-6 relate to judgment beginning at God’s house. John 21:15-17 records Peter’s commission to feed the sheep. Ezekiel 34 and John 10 speak of shepherds. Psalm 55:22 is the source of 5:7. Job 1-2 shows Satan with limits. James 4:6-10 has a similar sequence of humility and resisting the devil.
application:
Identify a gift God has given you, and put it to use in your church this week.

If you are in a hard season, repeat 5:7 and name the specific worry that you are handing to God.

Ask whether you are “watchful” or complacent. What habit would help you stay alert and resist the devil?
prayerPrompts: Cast your anxieties on God, and name them.
Ask him to help you resist the devil and stand firm.
Thank him for the grace that called you to eternal glory.
